title: Burst-to-Steady Transition Harness — Profiling Journal
content:
Purpose and context:
This is a working journal describing an experimental harness and methodology specifically focused on the transition from short bursts (microbursts) to steady-state throughput for the serving runtime. The goal is practical: produce repeatable runs that capture the transient behavior and identify dominant bottlenecks (scheduling, batching, KV cache warmup, GPU frequency/thermal throttling, memory pressure).

Why this matters:
- Many customer workloads exhibit spiky arrival patterns (user typing, background jobs, fanout). The worst-case tail and the time to reach efficient throughput both matter for cost and SLOs.
- Simple steady-state benchmarks miss the transition dynamics that cause higher unit-cost during ramping or after cold periods.

High-level hypothesis:
1) A significant portion of token-cost and latency variance during short runs is due to two orthogonal effects: (a) software-level priming (model and KV cache warming, batched-queue build-up) and (b) hardware-level transient behavior (GPU frequency ramp, power/thermal governors, memory allocation jitter).
2) A controlled, observable warmup procedure reduces variance and produces a deterministic baseline for evaluating batching and routing policies.

Load generator primitives (what the harness can do):
- Arrival profiles: poisson, fixed-interval burst, grouped microbursts, staircase ramp, and trace-replay.
- Payload primitives: variable seq-len distributions, prompt prefix reuse (to exercise KV cache), cached vs non-cached requests, and synthetic tokenization variants.
- Concurrency knobs: client-side concurrency, request pacing, max outstanding per-client, and grouped fanout.
- Environmental toggles: pin CPU affinity, set GPU governor (performance/ondemand), and enable/disable prefix cache.

Warmup and priming heuristics (practical rules used in experiments):
- Progressive primer: start with 50 short requests at low concurrency (C=2) to populate model weights and lazy allocations, then 5x bursts at moderate concurrency (C=8) to populate batched-queues and KV cache, then ramp to target load.
- Cache-aware reuse: send synthetic requests that reuse the same prefix keys at different sequence lengths to warm KV cache entries at both short and long key lengths.
- Thermal preconditioning: run a 10–20 minute low-latency priming phase that holds GPU utilization at ~40–60% to ensure GPU boosts are stable before high-intensity runs. This reduces frequency ramp noise.
- Seed-control: RNG seed the loadgen and, where applicable, the model sampling to eliminate run-to-run sampling variance for baseline runs. Document seed in run metadata.

Burst-to-steady transition detection (heuristics implemented in harness):
- Sliding-window occupancy: compute average GPU SM utilization, scheduler queue depth, and average batch size in 30s windows.
- Stabilization rule: consider steady-state reached when three consecutive windows have mean batch size within 5% and latency p95 within 10% of the running mean.
- Thermal guard: if GPU frequency varies more than 3% between windows, tag run as thermally-unstable and surface to analysis.

Thermal and GPU frequency considerations:
- Empirical observation: on our N cards, first 60–300s show transient frequency increases as power/thermal governors react; this creates apparent extra throughput in the early window.
- Practical mitigation: pin governor to 'performance' for critical runs OR run a fixed-duration 'preheat' that raises GPU temperature to target operating point. Document both options and compare.
- Log collection: record GPU frequency, temperature, power draw, and clocks every 5s and attach to run-level artifacts.

Runbook: orchestrated trial steps (scriptable):
1) Prepare environment: record git SHA of bench harness and model bundle, ensure drivers are up-to-date, note GPU model and BIOS, set governor if chosen.
2) Baseline allocation: run a single cold-start sample to capture the first-allocation cost (keep artifact).
3) Progressive primer: run the priming sequence (see heuristics) and mark end-of-priming timestamp.
4) Run trials: execute N trials (N>=5 recommended) of the target arrival profile; collect metrics at 1s granularity (latency distribution, batch sizes, queue depths, token/sec, model-side metrics).
5) Cooling interval: for tests that need cold restarts, provide a standardized idle window (e.g., 30m with daemon restart) and record.
6) Negative controls: run with KV cache disabled and with small batch cap to isolate impact of each subsystem.

Metrics and data to capture (minimum):
- Per-request: start_ts, end_ts, model_id, seq_len, batch_id, batch_size, latency (ms), trace_id.
- Aggregates: tokens/sec, requests/sec, mean/p50/p95/p99 latency, mean batch size, queue depth over time, executor CPU usage, GPU utilization, GPU frequency, power, temperature.
- Derived: time-to-stable (as defined above), variance decomposition components (sampling vs scheduling vs hardware).

Post-run analysis and variance decomposition approach:
- Align traces to priming end timestamp and compute per-second aggregates.
- Use change-point detection on batch_size and tokens/sec to identify abrupt transitions.
- Fit additive model: latency_variance ~ alpha*scheduling_variance + beta*batching_variance + gamma*thermal_variance + epsilon. Use controlled ablations to estimate coefficients (disable cache, fix batch cap, force governor).
- Produce visualization: waterfall plots showing contribution of each factor to p95 latency inflation during the first X minutes.

Actionable thresholds and decision rules (how to decide what to change):
- If time-to-stable > target_SLA_window (default 120s), then consider: increase primer intensity, enable longer preheat, or revisit autoscaler ramp policies.
- If thermal variance contributes >20% of latency variance, require hardware-level mitigation (governor change or thermal profile) before using host for deterministic benchmarks.
- If mean batch size stays below planned batching configuration for >30s, investigate queueing policy and client pacing.

Artifacts and reproducibility notes:
- Every run must include: bench harness config, git SHA, docker images list, system sysinfo (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=... snapshot), and the loadgen seed.
- Store run artifacts in the bench-run namespace with a unique run id and attach a short README describing anomalies.

Example loadgen snippet (YAML-like, for copy into our harness):
---
profile: burst_staircase
stages:
  - name: primer_small
    arrival: fixed
    rate: 10rps
    concurrency: 2
    duration: 60s
  - name: primer_bursts
    arrival: grouped_burst
    burst_size: 32
    interburst: 5s
    concurrency: 8
    repeats: 5
  - name: ramp_to_target
    arrival: linear_ramp
    start_rate: 50rps
    end_rate: 500rps
    duration: 120s
target_run:
  duration: 900s
  record_granularity: 1s
  seed: 20250315-001
---

Shell snippets used in experiments:
- start harness: ./bench-harness --config runs/primer_burst_staircase.yml --outdir artifacts/run-2025-03-15-001
- collect GPU logs: watch -n5 nvidia-smi --query-gpu=timestamp,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu,clocks.sm,power.draw --format=csv >> artifacts/gpu-log.csv &
- capture scheduler queue: ./tools/queue-probe --pid $RUNTIME_PID --out artifacts/queue.csv &

Open questions and next experiments:
- Quantify how much latency variance remains when combining primer + thermal preconditioning vs only one of them.
- Evaluate warmup sequences optimized by reinforcement (search for minimal primer that yields stable runs).
- Integrate model-internal metrics (KV cache hit-rate at per-token granularity) into the run dashboard.

Notes to reviewers:
- This file is a living journal; run ids and links to raw artifacts are attached in the linked_artifacts field when available. Please challenge the thresholds (5%/10% numbers) — they were chosen for initial runs and may need tuning per GPU family.

Signed-off-by: Aisha Kapoor (eng-serving-runtime)
